images.filename: South Devon Railway sea wall breach February 2014.JPG
images.caption: The breach in the South Devon Railway sea wall at Dawlish, Devon, England, February 2014. The damage was caused by gales and high seas on the night of 4 February and the railway track was left hanging over the breach. This photo was taken on 7 February after the track had been cut away: the cut sections with sleepers still attached can be seen lying in the gap.
images.alt: The breach in the South Devon Railway sea wall at Dawlish, Devon, England, February 2014. The damage was caused by gales and high seas on the night of 4 February and the railway track was left hanging over the breach. This photo was taken on 7 February after the track had been cut away: the cut sections with sleepers still attached can be seen lying in the gap.

images.filename: 2014 at Dawlish - damage to railway fence in Marine Parade.jpg
images.caption: Storms in February 2014 damaged the palisade fence alongside the railway in Marine Parade, Dawlish. The panels nearest the camera are merely badly buckled; the panels further along have been removed entirely and replaced by a temporary barrier.
images.alt: Storms in February 2014 damaged the palisade fence alongside the railway in Marine Parade, Dawlish. The panels nearest the camera are merely badly buckled; the panels further along have been removed entirely and replaced by a temporary barrier.

images.caption: Relaying railway track at Coryton Cove in Dawlish, Devon. Pre-assembled concrete sleepers have been delivered to the worksite (between Coryton and Kennaway tunnels). The road-rail crane is moving a panel of these from the stockpile into its final position on the down line. The short temporary rails will then be removed and, when all the sleepers are in place, the permanent rails will be put in their place.
images.alt: Relaying railway track at Coryton Cove in Dawlish, Devon. Pre-assembled concrete sleepers have been delivered to the worksite (between Coryton and Kennaway tunnels). The road-rail crane is moving a panel of these from the stockpile into its final position on the down line. The short temporary rails will then be removed and, when all the sleepers are in place, the permanent rails will be put in their place.

images.caption: Storms in February 2014 closed the railway line at Dawlish for several weeks. This road-rail crane is going to collect new signalling cables from a lorry delivering them in Marine Parade and then take them up to the station.
images.alt: Storms in February 2014 closed the railway line at Dawlish for several weeks. This road-rail crane is going to collect new signalling cables from a lorry delivering them in Marine Parade and then take them up to the station.

images.caption: An Exmouth to Paignton service passes along the newly-rebuilt section of the sea wall at Dawlish in April 2014. It is formed by First Great Western's 153373 and 143612.
images.alt: An Exmouth to Paignton service passes along the newly-rebuilt section of the sea wall at Dawlish in April 2014. It is formed by First Great Western's 153373 and 143612.

images.caption: The sea wall north of Dawlish station was breached on 4 February 2014. Although work had progressed sufficiently by April 4 to allow train services to resume, the footpath between Dawlish and Dawlish Warren remained closed at that time.
images.alt: The sea wall north of Dawlish station was breached on 4 February 2014. Although work had progressed sufficiently by April 4 to allow train services to resume, the footpath between Dawlish and Dawlish Warren remained closed at that time.

images.caption: When Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the sea wall at Dawlish in the 1840s he was not allowed to implement a track-level footpath along the whole route. Residents of Sea Lawn Terrace at Dawlish insisted that the footpath be carried at beach level in front of their houses. This section of the sea wall was breached by a storm on 4 February 2014. Ballast-filed shipping containers were placed on the footpath to provide some protection while rebuilding took place. The core of the wall had been completed and track relaid to allow train services to resume on 4 April but work still continued for a while after this date.
images.alt: When Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the sea wall at Dawlish in the 1840s he was not allowed to implement a track-level footpath along the whole route. Residents of Sea Lawn Terrace at Dawlish insisted that the footpath be carried at beach level in front of their houses. This section of the sea wall was breached by a storm on 4 February 2014. Ballast-filed shipping containers were placed on the footpath to provide some protection while rebuilding took place. The core of the wall had been completed and track relaid to allow train services to resume on 4 April but work still continued for a while after this date.

images.caption: When the sea wall north of Dawlish station was reopened in April 2014 there was still work to be done to finish the job. This view, taken eight days after train services resumed, shows a distinct dip in track level where the new wall has been constructed. A temporary speed restriction of 30 mph is in place through here, easing to 60 (35 for trains with heavier suspensions) just beyond the dip.
images.alt: When the sea wall north of Dawlish station was reopened in April 2014 there was still work to be done to finish the job. This view, taken eight days after train services resumed, shows a distinct dip in track level where the new wall has been constructed. A temporary speed restriction of 30 mph is in place through here, easing to 60 (35 for trains with heavier suspensions) just beyond the dip.

images.caption: The sea wall was reopened on 4 April 2014, two months after it had been severely damaged by storms. Despite this there remains much work to be done. First Great Western's 150130 (working from Exmouth to Paignton) is negotiating the breached section at Sea Lawn Terrace but more work can be seen beyond Rockstone bridge where scaffolding has been erected from beach level and shuttering is being prepared to cast a new section of the inner wall which separates the railway from the footpath between Dawlish and Dawlish Warren.
images.alt: The sea wall was reopened on 4 April 2014, two months after it had been severely damaged by storms. Despite this there remains much work to be done. First Great Western's 150130 (working from Exmouth to Paignton) is negotiating the breached section at Sea Lawn Terrace but more work can be seen beyond Rockstone bridge where scaffolding has been erected from beach level and shuttering is being prepared to cast a new section of the inner wall which separates the railway from the footpath between Dawlish and Dawlish Warren.

images.filename: 2014 at Rockstone - joint between stone and concrete wall.JPG
images.caption: Repairs to the South Devon Railway sea wall north of Rockstone Footbridge following the storms of February 2014. Where the parapet wall needed to be rebuilt the stones were replaced by concrete. The track side of the new wall is flat but the side facing the footpath has been cast using a mould of surviving stonework.
images.alt: Repairs to the South Devon Railway sea wall north of Rockstone Footbridge following the storms of February 2014. Where the parapet wall needed to be rebuilt the stones were replaced by concrete. The track side of the new wall is flat but the side facing the footpath has been cast using a mould of surviving stonework.

The Heritage Site is also called the Jurassic Coast, although Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods are represented.
